name: Trager approach

lead: The Trager approach is a form of somatic education developed by Milton Trager (1908-1997). A practitioner uses gentle, rhythmic rocking and lengthening movements on a clothed client on a table, with the aim of releasing habitual tension and teaching the body easier movement.
For appearance, the link is indirect: proponents describe looser, more relaxed posture, freer movement and reduced stress.

paras: Sessions last roughly 60 to 90 minutes. A second part, Mentastics, is a set of simple self-directed movements clients practise to reinforce the sensations of the table work.
The approach is gentle and non-invasive. It is not widely recommended in mainstream medicine for specific conditions, and published studies are small.

chain: Freer, more relaxed movement and posture
angle.text: Practitioners describe the work as teaching the body to move with less effort. People use it to loosen stiffness and tension that affect posture and carriage.

lead: The Trager approach, originally called Psychophysical Integration, is a bodywork and movement-education method created by Milton Trager, an athlete, dancer and bodybuilder who later trained as a physician. It combines passive, rhythmic table work with Mentastics, simple movements clients practise on their own.[1][2]

Proponents say it releases deep-seated physical and mental patterns, promotes deep relaxation and improves mobility and mental clarity. People interested in posture, movement quality and a relaxed physical presence describe using it for those reasons.[1][2]
Trager began teaching publicly at the Esalen Institute in 1975; the United States Trager Association was established in 2002. Research consists mainly of small studies.[2]

paras: During a session the client lies clothed on a table while the practitioner uses gentle bouncing, rocking, stroking and elongating movements. Practitioners enter a meditative state they call hook-up. Mentastics are movements clients practise at home.[1][2]

Trager developed the method from his own movement experiments and informal bodywork beginning in the 1920s, later practising medicine in Hawaii. He taught at Esalen from 1975 for the last 22 years of his life, and the Trager Institute was founded in the 1980s.[1][2]

Proponents report improved mobility, balance and coordination, reduced pain and stiffness and relief from stress, and they have applied it to conditions including Parkinson's disease, multiple sclerosis, post-polio syndrome and chronic headache.[1][2]

A randomized trial compared acupuncture and Trager Psychophysical Integration for chronic shoulder pain in wheelchair users with spinal cord injury.[3] A small randomized pilot of 33 volunteers examined Trager for chronic headache.[4] A 2021 case report described Trager for foot drop,[5] and a 1997 review covered it among holistic manual therapies.[6] Descriptions note that studies are small and often unblinded, and that the approach is not widely recommended in mainstream medicine.[2]

timeline.event: Milton Trager begins teaching publicly at Esalen.[2]
